intro: This is the opening number of the Dies irae sequence in Verdi’s Messa da Requiem. It begins with four orchestral blows, and the chorus moves from a full-throated cry to a murmur.

sections.label: A · Four strokes; chorus over rushing strings
sections.mNote: Rushing strings accompany the chorus’s cry of judgement

sections.label: A′ · Chorus repeats Dies irae over strings
sections.mNote: Single choral parts repeat “Dies irae” above the strings

sections.label: B · Repeated syllables over pizzicato bass
sections.mNote: Repeated syllables, plucked bass notes and short rising string runs.

cues.title: Opening of the Dies irae
cues.text: Four separated G minor chords come before the rushing strings and the chorus’s cry, “Dies irae” (“Day of wrath”). Verdi marks the movement Allegro agitato. The bass drum strokes fall across the beat, and the orchestral runs continue under the voices with few breaks.
cues.evidence: Verdi, Requiem, Eulenburg full score, plate E.E.4864, pp. 21–24, opening of No. 2. Latin words from the medieval Requiem sequence; translation ours. Score: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/71/IMSLP407348-PMLP01812-Verdi_Requiem_whole.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Milan, 1874
cues.text: Verdi conducted his Requiem for the writer Alessandro Manzoni at the church of San Marco in Milan on 22 May 1874, the first anniversary of Manzoni’s death. Three days later the same singers performed the work at La Scala.
cues.evidence: Teatro dell’Opera di Roma historical archive, premiere details: https://archiviostorico.operaroma.it/concerto/messa-da-requiem/. The subsequent La Scala performance is documented in the performance history at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Verdi).

cues.title: Requiem for Rossini, 1868–1869
cues.text: After Rossini’s death in 1868, Verdi proposed a Requiem shared among Italian composers and wrote its last number, the Libera me. The performance, planned for 13 November 1869, never took place. In 1871 he told an admirer: “There are so many, many Masses for the Dead.”
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner’s programme note: Verdi’s contribution to the joint Rossini Requiem was the Libera me, the work was not performed as planned, and in 1871 he wrote to an admirer, “There are so many, many Masses for the Dead. It would be pointless to add one more.” https://geraldlarner.com/work/verdi-messa-da-requiem . BR-Klassik (Bayerischer Rundfunk, Susanna Felix, 2017): the Requiem was to be given in Bologna on 13 November 1869, the first anniversary of Rossini’s death; the score was finished in time and the performance did not happen: https://www.br-klassik.de/themen/klassik-entdecken/messa-per-rossini-verdi-urauffuehrung-platzt-was-heute-geschah-1869-100.html

cues.title: Quantus tremor, chorus sotto voce
cues.text: “Quantus tremor est futurus” — “How great the trembling will be.” The chorus repeats its notes pp, marked sotto voce. Violins and cellos alternate short runs above pizzicato violas and basses.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg full score, pp. 39–42, Quantus tremor: choral pp and sotto voce, viola and bass pizzicato, alternating violin and cello figures. Latin sequence, translation ours.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Diminuendo to separate pp cupo entries
transitions.from: A · Four strokes; chorus over rushing strings
transitions.to: A′ · Chorus repeats Dies irae over strings
transitions.how: The bass holds G while the orchestral chords diminuendo. The brass stop. Clarinet and bassoon continue their scales. The choral parts enter separately, marked Soli and pp cupo (darkly), and repeat “Dies irae” above the strings. Up to this point the full chorus has sung the words together.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg full score, pp. 36–38: sustained G bass, diminuendo, and separate choral entries marked Soli and pp cupo.

transitions.title: Pizzicato strings and the “Quantus tremor” entry
transitions.from: A′ · Chorus repeats Dies irae over strings
transitions.to: B · Repeated syllables over pizzicato bass
transitions.how: Violas and basses play pizzicato, and violins and cellos alternate short upward runs. Low brass hold sustained notes beneath short woodwind chords. The chorus enters pp sotto voce on “Quantus tremor”, repeating syllables over the moving accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg full score, pp. 39–42, orchestral preparation and Quantus tremor entry.

source.title: Verdi, Requiem — Eulenburg full score, plate E.E.4864
source.locator: PDF pages 21–42, opening Dies irae number. “Tuba” represents the score’s ophicleide/bass-brass staff, not a verified instrument used in this transfer. No solo singers occur in this number; the offstage trumpets belong to the following Tuba mirum.

timeline.note: Four orchestral blows and rushing figures; the chorus enters after the opening attacks.
Choral entry region; lower and upper voices enter in succession.
Expanded opening declamation, including bass-drum punctuation in the written score.
Diminishing region with progressively reduced scoring; not every group sounds continuously.
Quiet Quantus tremor region: repeated choral notes, active strings and restrained wind support.

composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: Composer whose catchy tenor tunes could carry a fatal meaning when the wrong man heard them.
facts: Provesi in Busseto; private lessons with Lavigna after Milan’s Conservatoire rejected him
Milan · Venice · Florence · Rome · Naples · Paris · St Petersburg · Cairo
Piave, Cammarano and Boito were his principal collaborators
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred music, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Milan’s Conservatoire turned Giuseppe Verdi down in 1832. Antonio Barezzi, a merchant from Busseto who had helped pay for his move to Milan, kept supporting him, and Verdi studied privately with Vincenzo Lavigna, formerly a musician at La Scala. He learnt counterpoint and went to the theatre. Four years later he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took a municipal musical post in Busseto. His patrons had known him since he was a boy and had heard him play, and they supported him with their own money.

His parents kept an inn and shop at Le Roncole, where he was born in 1813. He learnt the organ locally, then studied with Ferdinando Provesi in nearby Busseto. Oberto, his first opera, reached La Scala in 1839 and earned him further commissions. His daughter Virginia had died in 1838; his son Icilio died in 1839, and his wife Margherita in June 1840, when Verdi was twenty-six. That September the theatre presented his comedy Un giorno di regno, which failed.
